rules_evaluated.rule_lead: No time-of-day anchors in body prose.
rules_evaluated.evidence: L13: "Do it this week rather than on the morning of Module 1." This is not one of the banned deictic-to-now anchors (tomorrow / this morning / overnight / tonight), which assume a fixed clock relationship between when the line is READ and when the session happens. "The morning of Module 1" instead names the module event itself, matching the rule's own recommended fix pattern ("replace with module names"). Residual wrinkle noted: it still attaches a time-of-day word to that event, which would read slightly oddly for a cohort whose Module 1 runs in the afternoon or evening; reported as a todo rather than a violation because the meaning survives ("don't wait until the last minute") even when the literal time-of-day is wrong for a given cohort.

rules_evaluated.rule_lead: The curriculum does not narrate itself — subject test, then deletion test.
rules_evaluated.evidence: L7 "The training is hands-on from minute one" names "the training" as grammatical subject, which is the shape this rule targets for a cut. Deletion test: removing it and reading "We start Module 1... on [date]. You'll be writing real code on your real repo, with Claude Code running on your laptop, the whole way through" reads cleanly, which is the rule's own tell for NVA. Counter-consideration that keeps this inside: the deleted clause's specific claim ("from minute one", i.e. no ramp-up) is not restated by the surviving sentence, which emphasizes duration ("the whole way through") rather than onset — so the cut would silently drop the one actionable expectation (be ready to code immediately, not eased in) that the rest of the paragraph doesn't carry. Genuinely close call; recorded as a judgement PASS rather than N/A because the tension is real.
